title: The Coaching-School Reckoning: When Classrooms Must Own What Entrance Exams Test
content:
Hi [Name],

A structural shift surfaced across education communities this week that many school leaders will recognise — even if their September timetable has not caught up.

A central panel examining India's school-to-entrance-exam pathway proposed what forums have debated for years: cap commercial coaching at two to three hours daily, align board curricula with JEE and NEET depth, and give board marks more weight in admissions. The diagnosis is simple. Schools teach one thing. Competitive exams test another. Families bridge the gap with parallel coaching — often through arrangements schools cannot see or govern.

Teacher communities echoed a parallel strain: technostress. Burnout is rising not only from student behaviour, but from layering AI tools, dashboards, and compliance platforms without protected integration time. New mandates arrive every term. Classroom minutes stay the same.

Phone-ban research reinforced the lesson. Collecting devices calms rooms — but year-one academics barely move. Primacy is a design problem, not a pouch problem.

Schools that rebuild trust will own competitive foundations inside regular periods — and communicate that story before coaching centres own the parent narrative.

EduHexa has supported 100+ institutions through integrated-program positioning and parent-trust messaging — with partners seeing up to 129% admission increases when public voice matched classroom reality.
